newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Battered JKX sees 1997 turnaround.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Battered JKX sees 1997 turnaround.

text.p: Britain's JKX Oil & Gas Plc has had a hard time, hit by several major setbacks in Ukraine, but the minnow's new chief executive says better times lie ahead.
"I believe we are at a turning point for this company," said Bob McCrackin in his first interview since becoming chief executive of JKX in February.
It must be welcome news to investors, who have seen shares in JKX, which is also active in Georgia, fall steadily from their 190 pence flotation price in 1995.
The stock nose-dived in March when JKX announced a 14 million stg rights issue at 34 pence per share.
JKX says it has now sorted out its finances, but more importantly its Ukrainian joint venture has found customers who are likely to pay their gas bills.
"We believe we have entered into a phase where we have credit-worthy buyers," said McCrackin.
Solvent customers are hard to come by in the Ukraine, where JKX is active through the Poltava Petroleum Company (PPC) in which it has a 49-percent stake.
PPC produces gas and oil at the Novo-Nikolaevskoye complex in central Ukraine, in which JKX has an interest of 89 million barrels of oil equivalent in proven and probable reserves.
PPC fell on hard times last year when the buyer of its gas could no longer operate as a distributor after Ukraine decided only domestic firms were allowed to sell gas to end-users.
PPC was consequently forced to store its gas. It only continued delivering small amounts to a Poltava train components producer as part of a barter deal which still needs to be worked out.
But PPC's outlook has meanwhile improved through its contacts with Ukragas, which is part of state-owned gas producer and distributor Ukragasprom.
Through Ukragas, PPC signed contracts with six Ukrainian regions -- or "oblasts" -- for delivery of gas to schools, hospitals and other public organisations.
While many companies are broke, the oblasts are in a far healthier financial state, McCrackin said.
"The credit-worthiness that we see is that we are dealing with state-run entities such as schools and hospitals. The credit risk is as good as you can get," he said.
But he acknowledges that JKX's business environment still has its risks. Despite the contacts with Ukragas, there is no guarantee that the oblasts will continue to buy PPC gas.
A further uncertainty is another imminent change in the Ukrainian gas market.
The local press has reported that the President's office is seeking greater competition among distributors, but it remains unclear how that might affect Ukragas or Ukragasprom.
Against this backdrop of new oblast contracts and remaining uncertainties, McCrackin said: "We are optimistic, but also realistic about the future."
Meanwhile, McCrackin is looking for Western partners to co-operate in a project off-shore Ukraine's autonomous Crimean peninsula.

As tensions between Russia and the Ukraine over the mostly Russian-populated peninsula appear to be subsiding, JKX wants to expand its offshore licence to around 6,800 square kilometres from about 2,500.
The company wants to shoot a seismic programme over the expansion and seeks a partner to share the exploration risks with its local partner Chernomorneftegas.
"The Black Sea is a huge province for exploration that is as yet untapped," McCrackin said.
JKX earlier this week said it agreed a deal that will allow Atlantic Richfield Co to farm its interest in the Georgian sector of the Black Sea.
